narrative.summary: Ghana governs AI through its National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2035, launched by the President on 24 April 2026, which proposes a Responsible AI Authority, and through the Data Protection Act 2012, which regulates decisions based solely on automated processing. The Bank of Ghana's 2026 Cyber and Information Security Directive is the first binding sector rule on AI, requiring banks to govern AI and machine-learning systems and secure them. Government consultation drafts from 2025 would go further: a new Data Protection Bill, an Emerging Technologies Bill with an AI division, a Cybersecurity (Amendment) Bill on AI security standards, an Electronic Transactions Bill on automated decisions and recommender systems, and a bill on misinformation and deepfakes. None has reached Parliament.
lead_institutions: Ministry of Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations
narrative.review_notes: This review was first completed on 12 October 2026 and redone in a longer pass on 13 October 2026, covering Parliament's bills, acts and legislative instruments lists, the ministry's posts, each line ministry and each sector regulator, and the strategy's launch date now comes from the ministry's own launch article. Not yet verified from the official text: any AI material from the standards authority and the medicines regulator, and a 2026 Criminal Offences (Amendment) Bill. A Bank of Ghana AI directive under development, the national AI in education policy and the Responsible AI Authority are tracked as leads.

instruments.current_status: Cover dated December 2025. Launched by the President in Accra on 24 April 2026 (Ministry launch article on moc.gov.gh, and the Minister's launch remarks); the Minister told the National Data Protection Conference on 2 March 2026 that Cabinet had approved it. A separate 104-page appendices volume is published on moc.gov.gh. Next steps named by the Minister: a National AI Delivery Roadmap/Framework (still being developed per his 9 September 2026 speech) and an Emerging Technologies Bill (see leads and drafts). A Ministry post of 29 April 2025 titled 'Ghana Launches National AI Strategy' concerned the launch of the strategy's stakeholder consultation forum, not the strategy itself. Not yet verified from the official text: an earlier 'National AI Strategy 2023-2033'.
instruments.summary: Ghana's first official national AI strategy, a ten-year roadmap ('Ghana 2035: The AI-Powered Society') built on the Digital Economy Policy and Strategy and the Ghana Integrated Digital Transformation Blueprint. It sets an action plan under eight pillars (AI education, youth and jobs, digital infrastructure, data access and governance, the AI ecosystem, sector adoption, applied research and public-sector adoption), including reviewing intellectual-property law and calling for AI sandboxing environments. It recommends establishing an independent Responsible AI Authority in the first year, incubated by the Data Protection Commission, to coordinate implementation and lead quarterly monitoring.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Main national AI policy document; proposes the national AI governance body (Responsible AI Authority).

instruments.summary: Ghana's general data protection law, which establishes the Data Protection Commission and regulates the obtaining, holding, use and disclosure of personal data, with registration duties for data controllers. Section 41 gives individuals the right to require that decisions significantly affecting them are not based solely on automatic processing of their personal data, and obliges controllers to notify individuals of such decisions and reconsider them on request within 21 days, with exceptions for contracts and decisions authorised by law.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Data protection law governing personal data used in AI systems, with rights on solely automated decisions (s.41).

instruments.summary: Draft bill to replace the Data Protection Act, 2012 by establishing a Data Protection Authority and updating data subject rights. Clause 53 ('Application of Emerging Technologies') requires technology-driven decisions affecting data subjects to be explainable, contestable and subject to human oversight, empowers the Authority to regulate such processing and conduct risk assessments, requires bi-annual audits of such systems in critical sectors (health, energy, finance, government services and others) and a mandatory data protection impact assessment before launching personalised services that rely on emerging technologies. Clause 65 adds a right not to be subject to solely automated decisions including profiling, listing chatbots, 'emerging technology systems' and facial and emotional recognition as automated processing; 'emerging technologies' is defined to include artificial intelligence.

instruments.summary: Draft bill to establish an Emerging Technologies Agency, with an Artificial Intelligence Division among others, to promote and facilitate the adoption of emerging technologies and provide harmonised rules on their obligations, rights, ethics and safety. It sets guiding principles for emerging technology systems covering democratic integrity, non-discrimination and bias, transparency and oversight, personal data protection, accountability, reliability, risk and impact management (identification and mitigation of risks to human rights, democracy and the rule of law), human oversight, misinformation, security and a right to redress, with enforcement and regulation-making powers.

instruments.summary: Draft amendment to the Cybersecurity Act, 2020 (Act 1038) put to public consultation by the Cyber Security Authority. A new section 4A would give the Authority power to establish standards for certifying the security of innovative products including Artificial Intelligence, cloud, quantum computing, big data, IoT and blockchain, and to certify their security against those standards; section 59 would be amended to allow regulations on such certification. The draft also expands the Authority's investigative and prosecutorial powers over cybercrime.

instruments.summary: Draft replacement electronic transactions law published by the Ministry with its October 2025 package of draft sector bills. Clause 16 requires platforms and service providers using automated decision-making, algorithmic curation, profiling or recommendation systems to disclose key parameters, logic and potential impacts, inform users how such systems affect access to goods, services or content, and allow opt-outs from personalised recommendations; it empowers the Minister to issue guidelines or regulations for the ethical use of AI and automated systems. Very large platforms and search engines must also publish biannual transparency reports covering their use of AI tools for content moderation and algorithmic disclosure.

instruments.summary: Draft bill on false information and hate speech published by the Ministry for public consultation. It expressly covers Artificial Intelligence-generated statements and materials, defines 'Artificial Intelligence' for misinformation purposes to include deepfakes, bots and manipulated algorithms, and requires media houses with online presence and internet intermediaries to carry out annual human rights due diligence on risks linked to their algorithmic systems and content moderation, with administrative penalties for non-compliance. Ministries, public institutions, media houses and intermediaries must also perform annual misinformation and disinformation risk assessments.

instruments.current_status: Issued (cover dated March 2026) and officially launched by the Governor as the Bank's revised Cyber and Information Security Directive (CISD) 2026 (Governor's launch speech on bog.gov.gh; the launch date is not stated on that page). The text states no commencement date. Applies to banks, specialised deposit-taking institutions and development finance institutions. The Governor said on 9 October 2026 that a separate AI directive for the financial sector is being developed (listed under Leads).
instruments.summary: Revised binding directive of the Bank of Ghana, issued under the Bank of Ghana Act and the Banks and Specialised Deposit-Taking Institutions Act, setting cyber and information security requirements for regulated financial institutions. It requires institutions that use AI or machine-learning models in core processes such as credit scoring, fraud detection or customer interaction to implement governance, security and risk controls (bias reduction, explainability, auditability), set up an AI/ML oversight committee reviewing model risk assessments and adversarial testing, run AI/ML awareness training up to board level, and include transparency, audit, liability and dispute-resolution clauses in contracts for AI, ML or algorithmic services. Part XIX sets cybersecurity requirements for AI systems, including model-specific testing, and Annex E gives AI/ML governance and control guidelines.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Binding financial-sector rules on AI/ML governance, security and third-party AI contracts.
